why_how.text: Defensive driving keeps you aware and ready, since ninety-four percent of serious crashes trace to human choices and errors.
First, think safety: shun aggression and inattention, bank space ahead, and belt against ejection.
Second, stay aware: sweep mirrors often, read twenty to thirty seconds ahead, and keep eyes roaming.
Dodge aggressive drivers by slowing, pulling over, or exiting safely, while tracking walkers, riders, and animals.
Third, trust no one: expect red-light and stop-sign runners and plan every move for the worst case.
Fourth, hold the three- to four-second gap for reaction room.
Fifth, temper speed to conditions below ideal-road limits, since pace erodes control when trouble strikes.
Sixth, bank an escape route: sit seen and seeing with an alternate path for sudden blocks.
Seventh, kill distractions and grant driving your whole mind.
Human error drives ninety-four percent of bad crashes, while safety-first habits blunt it.
Mirrors and long scans feed awareness, while aggressive drivers get dodged by slowing or exiting.
Distrust plans for signal runners, while three-to-four-second gaps buy reaction time.
Low speed, escape routes, and full focus close the seven, while limits alone never suffice.

why_how.text: Broadcast presence and plans, since unseen and surprising moves cause crashes.
Headlights show you the dark and show you to others, so burn them through fog, rain, and snow, overriding auto lamps in bright snow glare.
Iowa law lights both beams sunset to sunrise and whenever sight drops to five hundred feet or less; wipers on means lights on.
Sound the horn for lane-drifting walkers and riders, passers swerving at you, inattentive or half-blind drivers, and blind alley mouths.
Also horn cars threatening you, anyone needing your presence announced, and your own runaway slides toward people.
Broken down, flee the roadway if able, blaze hazards, and park only where approaching eyes can see, never past crests or bends.
Stalled in a lane, march everyone out fast to ground far from shoulders and traffic, then call the authorities.
Presence and plans get broadcast, while headlights serve seeing and being seen.
Night and five hundred-foot murk mandate beams, while horns warn seven listed hazards.
Breakdowns flee roadsides with blazing hazards, while lane strandings march out and call.
